fields.Front: What does the "Atomicity" property of ACID guarantee?
fields.Back: A transaction's operations either all happen or none do — no partially-applied transaction is ever left committed.

fields.Front: What does the "Isolation" property of ACID guarantee?
fields.Back: Concurrent transactions produce a result equivalent to running them one at a time in some order, up to the chosen isolation level.

fields.Front: What does the CAP theorem state about a distributed data store?
fields.Back: It can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance at once — and since partitions will happen, real systems effectively trade off Consistency vs Availability.

fields.Front: In CAP theorem terms, why must a distributed system always effectively choose partition tolerance?
fields.Back: Network partitions will occur in any real distributed system, so a system that doesn't tolerate them simply fails during a partition — it isn't really an optional choice.

fields.Front: What is the N+1 query problem?
fields.Back: Fetching N parent records with one query, then issuing one additional query per parent to load related child data — N+1 total queries where a single join query would do.

fields.Front: In a Hibernate app like the ServiceOntario project, how does JPQL's JOIN FETCH fix an N+1 problem?
fields.Back: It eagerly loads the related entities in the same query via a join, instead of Hibernate lazily issuing a separate SELECT each time an association is accessed on a parent.

fields.Front: Besides JOIN FETCH, what Hibernate setting reduces N+1-style overhead when lazy loading is kept?
fields.Back: Tuning the Hibernate batch size (e.g. @BatchSize or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size), which batches multiple lazy-load queries into fewer IN-clause queries.

fields.Front: What's the main tradeoff of adding an index to a table?
fields.Back: Faster reads/lookups on the indexed column(s), at the cost of slower writes (inserts/updates/deletes must also update the index) and extra storage.

fields.Front: What's the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?
fields.Back: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in its own table; a foreign key is a column referencing a primary key in another table to enforce a relationship.

fields.Front: What is a database lock used for during a transaction?
fields.Back: To prevent other transactions from concurrently reading or writing the same data in a conflicting way, protecting consistency while the transaction runs.

fields.Front: What is denormalization, and why is it sometimes used despite violating normal forms?
fields.Back: Deliberately introducing redundant data (e.g. duplicating a column across tables) to reduce joins and speed up reads, trading write complexity and storage for query performance.

fields.Front: Give a concrete example of denormalization used to avoid N+1-style per-row lookups.
fields.Back: Storing a duplicated field — e.g. an order's customer name — directly on the order row instead of always joining to the customer table to fetch it.

fields.Front: What's the difference between ordinary lock contention and a deadlock?
fields.Back: Contention is transactions waiting for each other's locks and eventually proceeding; a deadlock is a cycle of transactions each waiting on a lock the other holds, which never resolves without the DB detecting it and aborting one.
Online Transaction Processing — optimized for many short read/write transactions, e.g. an order-entry system.
Online Analytical Processing — optimized for complex, read-heavy aggregate queries over large historical data, e.g. a reporting warehouse.

fields.Text: {{c1::1NF}} (First Normal Form) requires every column to hold atomic, indivisible values with no repeating groups.
{{c1::2NF}} requires 1NF plus no partial dependency — every non-key column must depend on the entire primary key, not just part of it.
{{c1::3NF}} requires 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key columns must depend only on the primary key, not on other non-key columns.
